opus-5.5.text:
I think the change will come more gradually than people imagine at first, and then suddenly it will feel like it was always there.

For work, the biggest shift is that execution becomes cheap. A lot of what we call work today is turning an idea into something real: writing the code, running the experiments, drafting documents, checking details. As models get stronger, much of that can be delegated. So what becomes scarce is judgment: knowing which problem is worth solving, what a good result looks like, and when something is subtly wrong. I see this even in research. The bottleneck is moving from "can we implement this" to "do we have the right taste and the right questions."

That also means the structure of teams could change a lot. One person with good judgment and a few strong AI agents might do what used to take a whole group. That's exciting, but it's also a real challenge, because many people's sense of value and identity is tied to the execution part of their job. Society will need to think seriously about how people transition, and how we define meaningful contribution.

For daily life, I hope AGI feels less like a tool you open and more like a very capable companion that understands your context: helping you learn anything at your own pace, handling the boring administrative parts of life, maybe giving people in places without good doctors or teachers access to that level of expertise. Equalizing access to high-quality knowledge could be one of the most important effects.

But I don't think humans become less important. If anything, things like curiosity, care for other people, and deciding what we actually want our lives to be about become more central. Machines can increasingly answer "how." The "why" is still ours.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll be honest, I try to resist the temptation to paint a very dramatic picture, because most of the people who have done that were wrong on the timeline and the details even when they were right on direction. But I do think the change is real, and I think it comes in a different order than people expect.

The first thing that changes is not that jobs disappear. It's that the unit of work changes. Right now a lot of knowledge work is really about translation, taking an intention and turning it into a document, a piece of code, a slide deck, an email that gets someone else to act. That translation layer is exactly what models are becoming good at. So the person's job shifts from producing the artifact to deciding what the artifact should be, and then judging whether what came back is actually right. Taste and judgment become the scarce thing. A junior engineer today might spend eighty percent of their time on implementation. In a few years they'll spend eighty percent of their time on specification and verification, and that's honestly a harder skill, not an easier one.

The second thing is that the gap between having an idea and testing it collapses. I think about this a lot from the research side. So much of what slows a lab down is not lack of ideas, it's that every idea costs a week of someone's time to try. When that cost drops close to zero, the bottleneck moves to compute and to knowing which questions are worth asking. I think you'll see the same pattern outside of AI, in biology, in materials, in anything where experiments can be simulated or automated.

For daily life, I actually think it's quieter than people imagine, at least at first. You won't wake up one day and everything is different. You'll just notice that the friction is gone from a lot of small things. Dealing with a hospital, understanding a contract, learning something you were curious about but never had the time for. The model becomes a kind of patient expert that's always available. And for a lot of people, especially people who never had access to a good doctor or a good teacher or a good lawyer, that's not a small thing. That might be the biggest equalizer we've had in a long time.

The part I worry about is the middle period. The technology moves faster than institutions do. Schools are still training people for the translation layer. Companies are organized around headcount doing that work. There's going to be a stretch, maybe five or ten years, where the capability is there but society hasn't rearranged itself around it, and that's where the real pain is. I don't think the answer is to slow the technology down. I think it's to be very deliberate about getting the benefits to people broadly rather than concentrating them. That's partly a technical question, about cost and open access, and partly a policy question, and I don't think either side can solve it alone.

So if you ask me what I expect, I'd say: work becomes more about judgment and less about production, daily life gets quietly easier in ways we'll stop noticing, and the hard part isn't the AGI, it's us keeping up with it.

astra-6.text:
I think AGI could change work by shifting our attention from carrying out tasks to deciding what is worth doing. If an AI can handle much of the research, analysis, and execution, then asking good questions, exercising judgment, and taking responsibility for the outcome become more important. That could give people more room to create, but it could also disrupt jobs. We shouldn’t assume that everyone will benefit automatically or adapt at the same speed.

In daily life, I imagine the change will feel less like using a new piece of software and more like having assistance available whenever you need it—whether you’re learning something, organizing your day, or trying to understand a difficult decision. But being capable doesn’t necessarily mean being trustworthy. People still need privacy, control, and the ability to question what the system tells them.

So I’m hopeful, but I don’t think the outcome is determined by the technology alone. A lot depends on how we make it accessible and how we support people through the transition. Ideally, greater intelligence should give people more freedom to choose how they live.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest change will be that intelligence becomes something people can access very easily. Today, when we want to do something, we’re often limited by what we know, what we can learn, or whether we can find someone to help. AGI could lower those barriers significantly.

At work, that means more than completing the same tasks faster. People may be able to take on projects that previously required an entire team. But jobs are collections of tasks, and those tasks will change at different speeds. There will be a difficult transition as people and organizations figure out where human judgment is most valuable and how to share the benefits.

In daily life, I hope we’ll see more personalized help with learning, navigating complex information, and handling routine responsibilities. That could give people more time and more independence, provided these systems are reliable and people retain control over important decisions.

I’m uncertain about the timeline. But I think we should start asking now: when the ability to execute becomes much cheaper, what do we choose to do? Knowing what matters, asking good questions, and taking responsibility for the outcome may become even more important.
